input.question: Low earth orbit speed is 15,430 mph to 17,450 mph. Escape speed must be higher. Why did it take Apollo missions three days to reach the moon, then, when it is only ~238,900 miles away?
input.ground_truth: Remember [Kepler's 2nd Law](_URL_1_) - orbits sweep out equal areas in equal time. For an elliptical orbit, such as a transfer orbit to the Moon, the effect of this law is that as you get further from Earth, the distance traveled along your orbit in a given time is less. So as the Apollo missions were traveling out to the Moon, they were constantly slowing down the entire time. By the time they were close enough to the Moon for the Moon's gravity to start pulling them inwards, [they were only traveling about 1113m/s](_URL_0_), or 2,489 mph.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Low earth orbit speed is 15,430 mph to 17,450 mph. Escape speed must be higher. Why did it take Apollo missions three days to reach the moon, then, when it is only ~238,900 miles away?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you want to throw a ball really far, all the way to your friend who is far away. But just throwing it hard isn’t enough—you also have to throw it in the right direction and not let the ground stop it.

Going to the Moon is a bit like that. Even though the Moon is not super far away (like 239 big steps if each step was a mile!), you can’t just go straight there super fast. 

Here’s why:

1. **You have to go sideways really fast!**  
If you just go straight toward the Moon, Earth’s gravity will pull you back down. So, you need to go really, really fast sideways (this is called "orbital speed") so you don’t fall back to Earth. That’s why rockets first go around Earth in a big circle a few times before heading to the Moon.

2. **You can’t just go straight like a car on a road.**  
If you drive a car from your house to a friend’s house, you can go straight. But in space, you have to follow special paths called “orbits.” To get to the Moon, you have to go up, then around, then up again, kind of like going around a big roundabout before getting to your friend’s house.

3. **It takes time to get the right speed and direction.**  
Rockets don’t go at the super-fast “escape speed” all at once. They go step by step: first, they get high above Earth, then they turn and go towards the Moon. It takes time to change direction and speed just right so they don’t miss the Moon.

So, even though the Moon is not that far away, it takes three days because the rocket has to go the right way, go really fast sideways, and follow the space road to get there safely! 🚀🌕
